sentences.show: In 216 BC, in southern Italy, one army trapped an army far bigger than itself, and killed tens of thousands of men in a single afternoon.
More than 2,000 years later, generals still study how.
This is the battle of Cannae. It began with a problem Rome could not solve. His name was Hannibal.
Two years earlier, the Carthaginian general Hannibal had marched an army over the Alps and into Italy.
He crushed the Romans at the river Trebia. Then again, at Lake Trasimene.
Rome panicked, and gave command to a dictator, Fabius, with a new plan. Do not fight Hannibal. Follow him. Starve him. Wear him down.
It worked. But Romans hated it. Hannibal was plundering Italy, and Rome’s allies began to wonder if Rome could protect them.
So Rome decided to end it. Its next two consuls were told to find Hannibal, and destroy him.
The Senate raised an army of unprecedented size. Eight legions, plus allies. Ancient writers count about 80,000 infantry, and 6,000 cavalry.
Hannibal had perhaps 40,000 to 50,000. Spaniards, Gauls, Libyans, Numidian horsemen, held together by loyalty to one man.
Ancient numbers are never exact. But everyone agrees: Rome had far more men.
Hannibal knew that head-on, Roman heavy infantry was superior. So he would not fight head-on.
But he had more cavalry, and better cavalry.
His plan was not to beat the Roman strength. It was to turn it against them.
On 2 August, by the Roman calendar, the armies met on a flat plain at Cannae, beside the river Aufidus.
The ground favored Hannibal. The river guarded one flank, and the Romans would face the morning sun, with dust in their eyes.
Before the battle, an officer named Gisgo called the Roman army astonishing. Hannibal reportedly replied: even more astonishing, in all those thousands, there is not one man called Gisgo.
Here is how the armies lined up.
The Romans packed their infantry deep, in a tight mass, to punch straight through the middle.
Cavalry guarded both flanks, and the river was on their right.
Hannibal did the opposite. In the center, his Spanish and Gallic infantry pushed forward, in a curve.
At the two ends, his best heavy infantry, the Libyans, held back, and waited.
By the river, his heavy cavalry. On the far side, the fast Numidians.
The battle began with the cavalry. By the river, Hannibal’s horsemen charged the Roman cavalry, and smashed it.
But they did not chase the survivors. They rode around behind the whole Roman army.
There, they hit the allied cavalry, and drove it from the field.
In the center, the infantry collided. The Romans pushed hard, and Hannibal’s curve bent backward, step by step.
It looked like his center was collapsing. The Romans poured in, packed tighter and tighter, until they could barely lift their swords.
And they never noticed the Libyans, standing at the sides of the trap.
Then Hannibal gave the signal. The Libyans turned inward, and struck both flanks.
The cavalry returned, and closed the rear. One of the earliest pincer movements in recorded history.
The Romans were inside a pocket, with no way out.
What followed was a massacre. The Greek historian Polybius says 70,000 Romans died. The Roman historian Livy says about 45,000.
Some modern historians think even that is too high. We simply do not know.
What is certain is who died: the consul Paullus, most of the senior officers, and about eighty senators or former magistrates.
Hannibal lost perhaps 6,000 to 8,000. The other consul, Varro, escaped with 70 horsemen.
In Rome, there was panic.
Rome declared a day of mourning. Almost every family had lost someone.
Most of southern Italy went over to Hannibal, and the king of Macedon pledged his support.
His brother Mago poured a pile of gold rings, taken from dead Romans, onto the floor of the Senate in Carthage.
His cavalry commander, Maharbal, begged him to march on Rome. Hannibal refused. Maharbal answered: you know how to win a victory, Hannibal. You do not know how to use one.
Historians still argue. Some say he was right: his army was in no state to besiege a city like Rome.
And Rome refused to negotiate. It raised new legions from landless peasants, even slaves, and banned the word peace.
A young officer named Scipio drew his sword on nobles who talked of fleeing, and made them swear to defend Rome.
Fourteen years later, at Zama, that same Scipio, with a reformed army, ended the war.
But Cannae became a model: the perfect battle of annihilation, where you surround the enemy completely.
Around 1900, Germany’s chief of staff, Alfred von Schlieffen, wrote that a modern battle of annihilation could follow Hannibal’s plan. It shaped the German plan for the First World War.
Dwight Eisenhower wrote that every commander seeks a battle of annihilation, and tries to repeat Cannae.
In 1991, General Norman Schwarzkopf cited Cannae as an inspiration for the Gulf War.
An outnumbered general taught the world how to win a battle in a day. And still lost the war.
So, was Cannae the perfect battle, or the most expensive victory in history? Tell us what you think.
Hannibal never reached Rome. The subscribe button is much closer. Take it.
